corpus_definition: Feeling unhappy because you want what someone else has.

forms.definition: an unhappy feeling because you want what another person has
forms.example: Her jealousy started when her sister got a better job.

syn.note: Very close. Envy is only about wanting what others have; jealousy can also be fear of losing someone you love.
Related: an angry feeling because you think something is unfair.

forms.note: No verb in this family. To say it as a verb, use 'envy' (a different word) or 'be jealous of'.

forms.definition: unhappy because you want what someone else has
forms.example: He felt jealous of his brother's success.

syn.note: Same meaning; a little more formal. 'envious of his success'.
Related: angry because you think something is unfair, not only because you want it.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you want what another person has
forms.example: She looked jealously at her friend's new phone.
forms.note: Also used for protecting something carefully: 'a jealously guarded secret'.

syn.note: Same meaning; a little more formal.

context.text: When Aziz bought a new car, his cousin felt a little jealous. He tried to hide his jealousy, but he kept looking at the car jealously all evening.

reviewer_note: No verb in this family; envy is a separate word and is mentioned only as a synonym/note. Jealousy also covers the 'afraid of losing a partner' meaning, noted in its syn note.

corpus_definition: Feeling sad or angry because you want what someone else has.
usage_note: be/feel/get jealous of + person or thing: 'She is jealous of her sister.' 'He is jealous of my new car.' Use 'of', not 'from' or 'on'.

relations.note: Same meaning and same pattern; a little more formal.
Related: angry because you think something is unfair.

context.text: My little brother is jealous of my new bike. I told him not to be jealous of me, because he can ride it on Sundays.

reviewer_note: Fixed adjective + preposition pattern; learner trap 'jealous from' mentioned in usage note.

corpus_definition: A public notice about a position that is open.
usage_note: a job advertisement for + job: 'a job advertisement for a teacher'. You see, read or answer a job advertisement; companies place or post one. Short form: job ad (informal).

relations.note: Common in American English, especially for online notices.
Related: the open job itself, not the notice about it.

context.text: I saw a job advertisement for an English teacher in Tashkent yesterday. I answered the job advertisement and sent my CV this morning.

reviewer_note: Noun phrase; no forms. British 'advert' / American 'ad' noted via job ad.

corpus_definition: Take part in an activity with other people.
particle_note: Not separable: 'join in the game' (not 'join the game in'). Often with no object: 'Everyone joined in.' Also 'join in with + noun': 'join in with the singing'.

relations.note: Same meaning; 'take part in' needs 'in' before the activity.
Similar, but often for longer activities or projects.
To not take part in a game or dance: 'I'll sit this one out.'

context.text: The children were singing in the yard, and Grandma joined in. Soon all the neighbours were joining in too.

reviewer_note: Inseparable phrasal verb; 'join in' vs plain 'join' (become a member) kept apart in particle note examples.

corpus_definition: to take someone away illegally by force and demand money

forms.definition: the crime of taking a person away by force, usually for money
forms.example: The police are investigating a kidnapping in the city.

syn.note: Same meaning; more formal, used in news and law.

ant.note: Saving a person who has been taken away.

forms.definition: the crime of taking a person away by force
forms.example: The kidnap of the businessman shocked the whole town.
forms.note: Mainly British; 'kidnapping' is more common everywhere.

forms.definition: to take someone away by force and ask for money to free them
forms.example: The businessman's son was kidnapped and held for ransom.
forms.note: British spelling doubles the p: kidnapped, kidnapping. American English also allows kidnaped, kidnaping.

syn.note: Same meaning; formal, used in news and law.
Related: take someone or something quickly by force.
Related: take something or someone suddenly by force; more general.

ant.note: To let a person go free.
To let a person who was kept as a prisoner leave.

forms.definition: taken away by force and kept by criminals
forms.example: The kidnapped girl was found safe after two days.

syn.note: Related: kept as a prisoner, for any reason.

people.definition: a criminal who takes a person away by force for money
people.example: The kidnappers asked for a large amount of money.

context.text: In the film, a rich man's son is kidnapped on his way to school. The police find the kidnapper quickly, and the kidnapping ends safely.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: double p in kidnapped/kidnapping/kidnapper (single p also allowed in American English). Noun kidnap kept as a British extra.

gate_overrides.msg_contains: noun 'kidnap': not in the dictionary as a noun
gate_overrides.reason: kidnap is a noun in the Oxford and Cambridge learner dictionaries ('the kidnap of a businessman', mainly British); WordNet 3.1 only lists the verb.

corpus_definition: to go down onto one or both knees on the ground

forms.note: No noun for the action. Kneel comes from 'knee' (the body part), but knee is a separate everyday noun, not a form of kneel.

forms.definition: to go down so that your legs are bent and resting on the ground
forms.example: She had to kneel to pick up the fallen coins.
forms.note: Past tense: knelt (British) or kneeled (American). Often 'kneel down'.

syn.note: Formal; kneeling for a short time to show respect, mostly in church.
Related: bend your legs low, but your feet stay on the ground.
Related: bend your head or body forward to show respect.

ant.note: To be up on your feet.
To get up from kneeling or sitting; a little formal.

forms.definition: with your legs bent and resting on the ground
forms.example: There is a statue of a kneeling woman in the park.

context.text: My little sister dropped her beads under the table. I knelt down to help her, and we stayed kneeling on the carpet until we found them all.

reviewer_note: Irregular past knelt/kneeled noted. Knee kept out of the forms (body-part noun, not a form of kneel).

corpus_definition: To not have enough of something.

forms.definition: a situation when there is not enough of something
forms.example: There is a lack of clean water in some villages.

syn.note: Not enough of something that people need, like water or doctors.
When something is not there at all.
Related: something you must have.

ant.note: A large amount, more than enough.
Formal: a very large amount of something.

forms.definition: to not have something, or not have enough of it
forms.example: They lack the money to buy a house.
forms.note: No preposition after the verb: 'lack money', not 'lack of money'. 'Lack of' is the noun.

syn.note: Related: you must have something; lack says you do not have it.
Related: feel sad because something is not there.

ant.note: Formal: to have or own something.

forms.example: Money was lacking, so the project stopped.
forms.note: Not used before a noun. Patterns: 'be lacking', 'lacking in + noun'.

syn.note: Not there; missing is more common in everyday speech.
Related: 'be short of money' = not have enough.

context.text: Our village school lacks computers. The teachers say the lack of equipment makes lessons hard, and good books are lacking too.

reviewer_note: Learner trap 'lack of money' as a verb phrase handled in the verb note (verb takes a direct object).

corpus_definition: a famous building or object that helps you find your way

forms.definition: a famous building or place that is easy to see and recognize
forms.example: The Eiffel Tower is a famous landmark.
forms.note: Also means a very important event: 'a landmark in history'. Often used before a noun: 'a landmark decision'.

syn.note: Related: a building or statue built to remember a person or event.
Related: 'the sights' are famous places tourists visit.
Related: any place people like to visit, not always a building.

context.text: The Registan in Samarkand is the city's most famous landmark. If you get lost, ask for the Registan and people will show you the way.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; land + mark is a compound, so no affix is claimed.

corpus_definition: a narrow road or a marked strip on a wide road

forms.definition: a narrow road, or one part of a big road marked with lines
forms.example: The driver stayed in the right lane on the highway.
forms.note: Also a marked strip for one runner or swimmer in a race.

syn.note: Related: road is the general word; a lane is narrow or is one part of a road.
Related: a very narrow street between buildings in a town.
Related: a narrow way for walking, not for cars.

context.text: My grandparents live at the end of a quiet lane outside Fergana. To get there, we drive in the left lane of the big road and then turn off.

reviewer_note: Both corpus senses (narrow road / marked strip) are covered by one map, as in the corpus definition.

corpus_definition: A person who is in charge of a group or organization.

forms.definition: a person who is in charge of a group, team or country

syn.note: The person in charge of a department, school or family.
The person with the highest rank; used in job titles.
Related: the person in charge of you at work.
Related: the person in charge of a sports team or a ship.

ant.note: A person who supports a leader or does what they say.

forms.definition: the position or skill of being in charge of a group
forms.example: Under her leadership, the team won three games.

syn.note: Related: controlling and organizing a business or group.
Related: help and advice about what to do.

forms.definition: to be in charge of a group and show people what to do
forms.example: He leads a team of ten engineers.
forms.note: Irregular: lead, led, led. Leader is made from this verb.

syn.note: Show people the way or help them decide.
Control and organize what people do.
Related: control a business or a group of workers.

ant.note: To do what a leader says or go after them.

forms.example: She works for a leading bank in Tashkent.

syn.note: Most important; very common and easy.
Best or most successful; a little informal.
Formal: the most important or famous.

context.text: Our class leader, Malika, leads every school project. Everyone likes her leadership, and she wants to work for a leading company one day.

reviewer_note: Person-noun headword stays the main noun entry; leadership as noun extra, lead as the source verb. Lead (metal, /led/) is a different word and left out.
